directAnswer: St. Miltiades, also spelled Melchiades, was pope from 311 to 314 and the first bishop of Rome to see the Church move from persecution to toleration under Constantine. In 313 he presided over a synod at the Lateran that judged the Donatist dispute in North Africa in favor of Bishop Caecilian of Carthage. Ancient sources describe him as African by birth, and his feast is kept on January 10.

sections.h2: From Persecution to the Edict of Milan
paras: Miltiades was elected in 311, after a vacancy that followed the exile of Eusebius. The situation of Roman Christians was already shifting: Maxentius, who controlled Rome, allowed property confiscated from the Church to be returned, and Miltiades sent deacons to recover it from the city prefect.

In October 312, Constantine defeated Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge. The following year, Constantine and his co-emperor Licinius issued the arrangement known as the Edict of Milan, granting Christians freedom of worship and the restoration of their churches. Miltiades thus became the first pope to lead the Roman church in the open, without fear of the state.

sections.h2: The Lateran Synod of 313 and the Donatists
paras: In North Africa, a party later called the Donatists refused to accept Caecilian as bishop of Carthage, claiming that one of his consecrators had betrayed the faith during persecution. They appealed to Constantine, who referred the matter to the bishop of Rome.

Miltiades convened bishops from Italy and Gaul in the autumn of 313. They met in a residence of the empress Fausta on the Lateran, property that soon passed to the Church and became the site of the papal cathedral. The synod upheld Caecilian and condemned Donatus. Miltiades reportedly sought a conciliatory settlement, offering to recognize bishops from the opposing side where only one claimant existed.

The Donatists did not accept the verdict, and the dispute continued at the Council of Arles in 314 and for generations afterward. Later Donatist polemic even accused Miltiades himself of having been a traitor during persecution, a charge St. Augustine took pains to refute.

The Liber Pontificalis calls Miltiades an African and attributes to him a rule against fasting on Sundays and Thursdays, along with other disciplinary decrees; historians treat such attributions cautiously, since the work was compiled centuries later.

He died in January 314 and was buried in the Catacomb of Callixtus. Though early lists sometimes counted him as a martyr, he died in peace at the very moment the age of the martyrs was closing, which gives his short reign its particular place in Church history.

keyFacts: Pope from 311 to 314; described as African by birth
First pope to serve after Constantine's victory and the Edict of Milan (313)
Presided over the Lateran synod of 313, which ruled against the Donatists
The synod met in the Lateran residence later given to the Church
Buried in the Catacomb of Callixtus; feast day January 10

faqs.question: Why is Pope Miltiades also called Melchiades?
faqs.answer: Both spellings appear in ancient manuscripts. Miltiades is the form generally preferred by historians, while Melchiades appears in many older Latin texts and calendars.

faqs.question: What did the Lateran synod under Miltiades decide?
faqs.answer: Meeting in 313 at the Lateran, the bishops under Miltiades confirmed Caecilian as the rightful bishop of Carthage and condemned the claims of Donatus, though the Donatist division in Africa continued long afterward.

faqs.question: Was Pope Miltiades a martyr?
faqs.answer: No. Some early lists honored him with martyr language, but he died peacefully in 314, after Constantine had ended the persecution of Christians.
